[00:00] Teacher (EN): Good morning, everyone. Sit down quickly, please. Bags under the desks. Thank you. Let's warm up. If I cut a sandwich into two equal pieces and eat one piece, what fraction did I eat?

[00:13] Student (EN): One half!

[00:16] Teacher (EN): One half, good. And four equal pieces, eating one?

[00:22] Student (EN): One quarter.

[00:25] Teacher (EN): Yes. And Lina, three equal pieces, eating one?

[00:30] Student 3 (EN): One third. Because there are three pieces and I ate one of them.

[00:36] Teacher (EN): Good. Which is bigger, one half or one quarter? Sam?

[00:42] Student 2 (EN): One half. When there are only two pieces, each piece is bigger.

[00:48] Teacher (EN): Right, fewer parts, bigger parts. Okay, the objective is on the board: we will add fractions with the same denominator. Read it with me.

[00:59] Student (EN): We will add fractions with the same denominator.

[01:04] Teacher (EN): Take a paper strip from the tray. It is marked into five equal parts, so fold along the lines. Each part is one fifth. Shade one part, then shade two more. How many fifths are shaded?

[01:19] Student (EN): Three fifths.

[01:22] Teacher (EN): Three fifths. The parts stay the same size, they are still fifths. We just count how many we have.

[01:29] Teacher (EN): Some people say one fifth plus two fifths is three tenths. Is that right? Ayo, check your strip. Is it in ten parts now?

[01:39] Student 3 (EN): No, still five. The pieces did not get smaller.

[01:44] Teacher (EN): Exactly. The denominator is the size of the parts. We never add the denominators.

[01:51] Teacher (EN): Watch the board. One fifth plus two fifths. Step one, the denominators match. Step two, add the numerators, one plus two is three. Step three, keep the five. Three fifths.

[02:05] Student (EN): Teacher, why does the five stay the same at the bottom?

[02:10] Teacher (EN): Because the pieces are still fifths. We changed how many pieces we have, not their size.

[02:17] Teacher (EN): Let me show one more on the board myself. Three tenths plus four tenths. Tens match, three plus four is seven, seven tenths. And another: two ninths plus five ninths, that is seven ninths. See how the bottom number never changes?

[02:34] Teacher (EN): Okay, let's try one together. Two eighths plus three eighths. What do you get?

[02:41] Student (EN): Five eighths.

[02:44] Teacher (EN): Good. Right, we are running short of time, so we will move on.

[02:49] Teacher (EN): Tomi, please stop tapping the desk. Thank you. Everyone, can I have quiet, please? I can hear chatting at the back table, and the class next door is having a test. And whoever left the strips on the floor, please pick them up. Monitors, collect the strips into the tray now.

[03:08] Student (EN): Teacher, can we keep our strips? I want to show my brother at home how fifths work.

[03:15] Teacher (EN): Not today, they go back in the tray. We need them for the other class after break. Quickly, please.

[03:23] Teacher (EN): Okay. Who can tell me today's rule in one sentence?

[03:28] Student 2 (EN): If the denominators are the same, add the numerators and keep the denominator.

[03:34] Teacher (EN): Yes. Say it with them, everyone. When the denominators are the same, add the top numbers and the bottom number stays.

[03:43] Teacher (EN): Your exit question is two sixths plus three sixths. Think about it on your way home.

[03:50] Teacher (EN): Right, homework. Write this in your diary first. Homework is in your workbook, page forty-two, questions one to five. Please do them neatly in pencil and show me tomorrow morning before assembly.

[04:05] Student (EN): All five questions? Even the ones with the big numbers at the bottom?

[04:11] Teacher (EN): All five. They are short. Remember, the denominator stays the same. Off you go, line up quietly at the door.
